concepts.label: The abducens nucleus lies in the floor of the fourth ventricle, so a fourth-ventricle tumour classically affects it first
concepts.article_title: Abducens nucleus and the fourth ventricle floor
concepts.definition: The abducens (CN VI) nucleus lies in the caudal pons, immediately beneath the facial colliculus in the floor of the fourth ventricle, with the looping fibres of the facial nerve (internal genu) wrapped around it. Because of this superficial, floor-facing position, an expanding mass in the fourth ventricle (such as an ependymoma or a pontine glioma bulging into the ventricle) compresses the abducens nucleus early, producing an ipsilateral lateral rectus palsy sometimes accompanied by ipsilateral facial weakness from the adjacent facial genu. This makes abducens palsy a classically taught localising sign of fourth-ventricle floor pathology.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that the abducens nucleus sits in the floor of the fourth ventricle and is therefore vulnerable to fourth-ventricle tumours.
concepts.module_subject: ASU-CNS-3 > Anatomy > Brainstem cranial nerve nuclei
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing the abducens nucleus's floor-of-the-fourth-ventricle location (vulnerable to intraventricular tumours) with the abducens nerve's separate vulnerability in the cavernous sinus or at the petrous apex (Dorello canal) further along its course.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 1 ("Tumor in 4th ventricle affects the Abducent nucleus"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf, p1.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 1 of EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf (src_85504e7525d793760af2), p1, answer/topic stated before the stem — this batch authors its own distractors.

concepts.label: Wernicke's area formulates the thoughts that are then converted into speech by Broca's area
concepts.definition: Wernicke's area, in the posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus of the dominant (usually left) hemisphere, is classically described as the general interpretative (gnostic) area where incoming auditory and visual language signals are analysed for meaning and where coherent thoughts are formulated. These formulated thoughts are then relayed, chiefly via the arcuate fasciculus, to Broca's area in the inferior frontal gyrus, which converts them into the motor programme for articulate speech. A lesion of Wernicke's area therefore produces fluent but meaningless (receptive/Wernicke) aphasia, because the patient can still produce speech sounds but has lost the capacity to formulate or comprehend coherent language content.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that Wernicke's area is responsible for formulating thoughts prior to their conversion into speech by Broca's area.
concepts.module_subject: ASU-CNS-3 > Physiology > Language and higher cortical function
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing Wernicke's area's role in formulating/comprehending the content of language with Broca's area's separate role in converting that content into the motor programme of articulate speech.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 2 ("Formation of thoughts in Wernicke's area"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf, p1.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 2 of EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf (src_85504e7525d793760af2), p1.

concepts.label: Alprazolam, a rapid-onset benzodiazepine, is used to abort an acute panic attack
concepts.definition: Alprazolam is a short-acting, high-potency benzodiazepine that binds the GABA-A receptor's benzodiazepine site, increasing the frequency of chloride channel opening and rapidly potentiating GABAergic inhibition. Its rapid onset of anxiolytic and sedative action makes it a first-line agent for terminating an acute panic attack, distinct from the longer-term, delayed-onset SSRIs used for panic disorder maintenance therapy. Because of its abuse and dependence potential, it is generally reserved for short-term or as-needed use rather than chronic daily dosing.
concepts.explicit_objective: Identify alprazolam as the benzodiazepine used to abort an acute panic attack.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing alprazolam's role in aborting an acute panic attack with the delayed-onset SSRIs used for chronic panic-disorder prophylaxis.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 4 ("Panic attack>alprazolam"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf, p1.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 4 of EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf (src_85504e7525d793760af2), p1.

concepts.label: The great cerebral vein (of Galen) is formed by the union of the two internal cerebral veins
concepts.definition: The great cerebral vein (of Galen) is a short, unpaired venous trunk formed beneath the splenium of the corpus callosum by the union of the two internal cerebral veins (which themselves drain the deep structures of the cerebral hemispheres), together with the paired basal veins of Rosenthal. It then curves backward and joins the inferior sagittal sinus to form the straight sinus. As a deep venous confluence, its thrombosis or malformation (e.g. vein of Galen aneurysmal malformation) has serious clinical consequences distinct from superficial cortical venous pathology.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that the great cerebral vein of Galen is formed by the union of the two internal cerebral veins.
concepts.subtopic: Venous drainage of the head and neck
concepts.module_subject: ASU-CNS-3 > Anatomy > Venous drainage of the head and neck
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing the great cerebral vein's formation from the paired internal cerebral veins with its own subsequent drainage into the straight sinus.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 5 ("Great cerebral vein>2 internal cerebral veins"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf, p1.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 5 of EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf (src_85504e7525d793760af2), p1.

concepts.label: The cingulum, deep to the cingulate gyrus, completes the Papez circuit by returning fibres from the cingulate gyrus toward the hippocampal formation
concepts.article_title: The cingulum in the Papez circuit
concepts.definition: The Papez circuit runs hippocampus to fornix to mammillary bodies to anterior thalamic nucleus (mammillothalamic tract) to cingulate gyrus (anterior thalamic radiation), and is completed by the cingulum, a white-matter bundle running within the cingulate gyrus that projects fibres from the cingulate cortex back down to the parahippocampal gyrus and hippocampal formation, closing the loop. This anatomical closure is what allows the circuit to recirculate and sustain emotional tone over time, distinguishing the cingulum's specific anatomical role from the circuit's overall function of prolonging and elaborating emotional experience.
concepts.explicit_objective: Identify the cingulum as the white-matter tract that completes the Papez circuit by connecting the cingulate gyrus back toward the hippocampal formation.
concepts.module_subject: ASU-CNS-3 > Anatomy > Limbic system and emotion
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing the cingulum (the white-matter tract within the cingulate gyrus that closes the Papez loop) with the mammillothalamic tract or the fornix, the circuit's other named component tracts.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 6 ("Papez circuit>cingulum"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf, p1.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 6 of EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf (src_85504e7525d793760af2), p1. This lane's own finalpaper2-2024 cluster already minted a separate concept for the Papez circuit's overall function (prolongation/elaboration of emotional experience) — this concept instead covers the cingulum's specific anatomical role in closing the loop, a distinct fact, not a re-mint of the same claim.

concepts.label: Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms, a consequence of chronic hypertension, are the classic cause of hypertensive intracerebral haemorrhage
concepts.definition: Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms are tiny (under 1 mm) aneurysmal dilatations that develop on the small penetrating (lenticulostriate and other perforating) arteries of the brain, chiefly in the basal ganglia, thalamus, pons and cerebellum, as a direct consequence of chronic, poorly controlled hypertension weakening the vessel media. Their rupture is the classic mechanism of primary (spontaneous) hypertensive intracerebral haemorrhage, distinguishing it from amyloid angiopathy-related lobar haemorrhage, which instead affects more peripheral cortical vessels in normotensive elderly patients. Their characteristic distribution in the basal ganglia/thalamus is why hypertensive bleeds are classically described as "deep" haemorrhages.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms, caused by chronic hypertension, are the classic mechanism of deep hypertensive intracerebral haemorrhage.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing hypertension-driven Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms of the deep perforating arteries with cerebral amyloid angiopathy, the other major cause of spontaneous intracerebral haemorrhage, which instead produces lobar (peripheral cortical) bleeds in normotensive elderly patients.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 7 ("Hypertension >Charcot aneurysm"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf, p1.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 7 of EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf (src_85504e7525d793760af2), p1. Printed key says "Charcot aneurysm"; standard terminology is Charcot-Bouchard aneurysm.

concepts.label: Sleepwalking (somnambulism) is a parasomnia of non-REM (slow-wave) sleep, not of REM sleep
concepts.definition: Sleepwalking (somnambulism) is a disorder of arousal that arises out of slow-wave (stage N3) non-REM sleep, typically in the first third of the night when slow-wave sleep predominates, and is characterised by complex motor behaviour with impaired consciousness and no memory of the episode afterward. This distinguishes it mechanistically from REM sleep behaviour disorder, in which the normal REM-sleep skeletal muscle atonia fails and patients physically act out vivid dreams. Because REM sleep is normally accompanied by near-total atonia, complex ambulatory behaviour during REM would require a specific atonia failure, whereas NREM sleepwalking instead reflects incomplete arousal from deep slow-wave sleep with preserved motor tone.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that sleepwalking is a disorder of non-REM (slow-wave) sleep, not REM sleep.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing NREM sleepwalking (a disorder of arousal from deep slow-wave sleep, motor tone preserved) with REM sleep behaviour disorder (dream enactment due to failure of the normal REM atonia).
concepts.original_wording: Source item 8 ("Non Rem :walking during sleep"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf, p1.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 8 of EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf (src_85504e7525d793760af2), p1.

concepts.label: The lingual artery passes deep to hyoglossus muscle on its way to the tongue
concepts.definition: The lingual artery, a branch of the external carotid artery, ascends in the carotid triangle and then passes deep to (medial to) the hyoglossus muscle within the digastric (submandibular) triangle before continuing forward to supply the tongue. This deep relation to hyoglossus is a key surgical landmark (Pirogoff's triangle), since retracting or removing hyoglossus is the standard step used to expose and ligate the lingual artery. The hypoglossal nerve, by contrast, runs superficial to hyoglossus, giving the two structures a useful anatomical contrast at this level.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that the lingual artery runs deep to hyoglossus muscle.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing the lingual artery's deep relation to hyoglossus with the hypoglossal nerve's superficial relation to the same muscle at the same level.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 9 ("Deep to hypoglossus:lingual artery"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf, p1.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 9 of EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf (src_85504e7525d793760af2), p1.

concepts.label: Oligodendroglioma cells characteristically show a clear perinuclear halo ("fried-egg" appearance) on histology
concepts.definition: Oligodendroglioma, a diffusely infiltrating glioma arising from oligodendrocyte-lineage cells (classically defined by IDH mutation and 1p/19q co-deletion), shows tumour cells with round, regular nuclei surrounded by a clear cytoplasmic halo on routine formalin-fixed sections, giving the classic "fried-egg" appearance. This halo is a fixation artefact, caused by swelling and clearing of the cytoplasm during tissue processing, rather than a true feature of the living cell, and is characteristically absent on frozen-section preparation. The tumour also typically shows a delicate "chicken-wire" capillary network, another supporting histological clue.
concepts.explicit_objective: Identify the clear perinuclear halo ("fried-egg" appearance) as the classic histological feature of oligodendroglioma on formalin-fixed sections.
concepts.pitfalls: Treating the perinuclear halo as a true living-cell feature rather than a formalin-fixation artefact, which is why it is characteristically absent on frozen section.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 18 ("Tumor cell with clear halo :oligodendroglioma"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf, p2.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 18 of EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf (src_85504e7525d793760af2), p2.

concepts.label: Herpes simplex virus encephalitis classically causes haemorrhagic necrosis of the temporal lobe
concepts.article_title: HSV encephalitis and temporal lobe necrosis
concepts.definition: Herpes simplex virus type 1 encephalitis has a strong predilection for the medial temporal lobes, insula and orbitofrontal cortex, producing characteristic asymmetric haemorrhagic necrosis of these regions, seen as temporal lobe hypodensity/haemorrhage on imaging and confirmed by CSF PCR for HSV DNA. Clinically this localisation explains the classic presentation of fever, altered consciousness, and temporal-lobe features such as olfactory or gustatory hallucinations, personality change and seizures. Untreated HSV encephalitis has very high mortality, which is why empirical IV aciclovir is started immediately whenever this diagnosis is suspected, before confirmatory testing returns.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that herpes simplex encephalitis classically produces haemorrhagic necrosis localised to the temporal lobes.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing HSV encephalitis's temporal-lobe predilection with other CNS viral infections (e.g. rabies affecting the brainstem/limbic system diffusely, or arboviral encephalitides without a temporal-lobe pattern).
concepts.original_wording: Source item 19 ("Necrosis at Temporal lobe : Herpes simplex virus"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf, p2.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 19 of EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf (src_85504e7525d793760af2), p2.

concepts.label: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy is caused by reactivation of JC virus, a polyomavirus, in immunocompromised patients
concepts.definition: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) is a demyelinating disease of the CNS caused by reactivation of the JC virus (a human polyomavirus, historically grouped with papillomaviruses in the "Papovaviridae" family) in severely immunocompromised patients, such as those with advanced HIV/AIDS or those on certain immunosuppressive/immunomodulatory drugs (e.g. natalizumab). The virus lytically infects oligodendrocytes, producing multifocal areas of demyelination, and typically presents with progressive focal neurological deficits, cognitive decline and visual disturbance without fever. It is a classic AIDS-defining opportunistic CNS infection, distinct from HIV-associated dementia itself.
concepts.explicit_objective: Identify JC virus, a polyomavirus, as the cause of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy in immunocompromised patients.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing JC virus (the polyomavirus causing PML by infecting oligodendrocytes) with other opportunistic CNS pathogens of immunocompromised patients, such as CMV or Toxoplasma.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 20 ("Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy : Papo virus"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf, p2.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 20 of EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf (src_85504e7525d793760af2), p2. Printed key abbreviates as "Papo virus P with P" (Papovavirus); modern classification places JC virus in Polyomaviridae.

concepts.label: The thalamus forms the greater part of the lateral wall of the third ventricle
concepts.article_title: Thalamus and the third ventricle lateral wall
concepts.definition: The lateral wall of the third ventricle is formed above the hypothalamic sulcus by the medial surface of the thalamus, and below the sulcus by the hypothalamus; the two thalami are frequently joined across the ventricle by the interthalamic adhesion (massa intermedia). This makes the thalamus the dominant structure forming the upper, larger part of the lateral wall, a fact used to explain why thalamic tumours or haemorrhage can obstruct the third ventricle and produce hydrocephalus. The roof of the third ventricle, by contrast, is formed by the tela choroidea and its choroid plexus, a distinct boundary.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that the thalamus forms the lateral wall of the third ventricle (above the hypothalamic sulcus).
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing the thalamus's role forming the lateral wall (above the hypothalamic sulcus) with the hypothalamus's role forming the lower part of the same wall, or with the choroid plexus/tela choroidea forming the roof.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 21 ("Lateral wall of third ventricle:Thalamus"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf, p2.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 21 of EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf (src_85504e7525d793760af2), p2.

concepts.label: The choroid plexus is formed by vascular pia mater (tela choroidea) invaginating the ependymal lining of the ventricle
concepts.definition: The choroid plexus develops where a fold of vascular pia mater, the tela choroidea, invaginates into the ventricular cavity and becomes covered by a single layer of specialised ependymal (choroidal epithelial) cells, so that each choroid plexus villus consists of a pia-derived vascular core wrapped in an ependymal-derived epithelium. This dual pia-plus-ependyma composition, distinct from either layer alone, is what allows the choroidal epithelium to actively secrete cerebrospinal fluid from the plexus capillaries' filtrate. The arrangement is present wherever choroid plexus occurs — the lateral, third and fourth ventricles.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that the choroid plexus is composed of vascularised pia mater (tela choroidea) covered by ependymal epithelium.
concepts.pitfalls: Naming only the vascular pial component (tela choroidea) or only the ependymal epithelium alone, rather than recognising the choroid plexus as the combination of both layers together.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 23 ("Choroid plexus :vascularized pia and ependyma"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf, p2.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 23 of EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf (src_85504e7525d793760af2), p2. A related but distinct AU-MED-203 concept covers choroid plexus CSF-secretion transport physiology, not this composition fact.

concepts.label: The medial geniculate body receives its main input from the inferior colliculus via the brachium of the inferior colliculus
concepts.article_title: Medial geniculate body and the inferior colliculus
concepts.definition: In the auditory pathway, ascending fibres from the inferior colliculus of the midbrain (the principal midbrain auditory relay) leave via the brachium of the inferior colliculus to terminate in the medial geniculate body (MGB) of the thalamus, the dedicated thalamic auditory relay nucleus. From the MGB, third-order fibres form the auditory radiation, which passes through the sublentiform part of the internal capsule to reach the primary auditory cortex (Heschl's gyrus) in the superior temporal gyrus. This inferior colliculus-to-MGB-to-cortex sequence is the thalamic relay step of the auditory pathway, parallel to how the lateral geniculate body relays vision.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that the medial geniculate body receives its principal input from the inferior colliculus via its brachium.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing the medial geniculate body (auditory thalamic relay, fed by the inferior colliculus) with the lateral geniculate body (visual thalamic relay, fed by the optic tract/superior colliculus).
concepts.original_wording: Source item 25 ("Medial Geniculate Body:inferior colliculus"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf, p2.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 25 of EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf (src_85504e7525d793760af2), p2.

concepts.label: The auditory radiation passes through the sublentiform part of the internal capsule to reach the auditory cortex
concepts.article_title: Auditory radiation and the sublentiform internal capsule
concepts.definition: The internal capsule is divided into anterior limb, genu, posterior limb, retrolentiform and sublentiform parts relative to the lentiform nucleus; the auditory radiation, carrying third-order fibres from the medial geniculate body to the primary auditory cortex (Heschl's gyrus), passes specifically through the sublentiform part, below the lentiform nucleus. This is classically contrasted with the optic radiation, most of which passes through the retrolentiform part, behind the lentiform nucleus, giving the two sensory radiations distinct topographic positions within the same capsule. Damage confined to the sublentiform region can therefore selectively affect auditory input from that hemisphere.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that the auditory radiation passes through the sublentiform part of the internal capsule.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing the sublentiform location of the auditory radiation with the retrolentiform location of the (mostly) optic radiation in the same internal capsule.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 26 ("SUblentiform: AUditory radiation"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf, p2.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 26 of EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf (src_85504e7525d793760af2), p2.

concepts.label: Purkinje cells are found in the cerebellar cortex, not the cerebral cortex
concepts.article_title: Purkinje cells belong to the cerebellum
concepts.definition: Purkinje cells are large, flask-shaped GABAergic neurons with an extensively branching dendritic tree confined to the molecular layer of the cerebellar cortex, where they form the sole output of the cerebellar cortex, projecting inhibitory axons to the deep cerebellar nuclei. They are not present in the cerebral cortex, whose principal projection neurons are instead pyramidal cells of the various cortical layers. This distinction is a classic "which cell type belongs where" histology question, testing whether the cerebellar-specific Purkinje cell is mistakenly attributed to the cerebral cortex.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that Purkinje cells are a cerebellar cortex cell type, not a cerebral cortex cell type.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing the cerebellar-specific Purkinje cell with the pyramidal cells that are the principal projection neurons of the cerebral cortex.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 26 (second, "cells not in cerebral cortex :purkinje fibers (In cerebellum)"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf, p3.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as p3 item 26 (renumbered after p2's item 26) of EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf (src_85504e7525d793760af2).

concepts.label: Conduction aphasia is characterised by an inability to repeat spoken words despite intact comprehension and fluent speech
concepts.definition: Conduction aphasia results from a lesion of the arcuate fasciculus, the white-matter tract connecting Wernicke's area (language comprehension) to Broca's area (speech production), disconnecting the two while leaving each individually intact. Patients therefore have fluent, grammatically normal speech and largely preserved auditory comprehension, but are strikingly unable to repeat spoken words or phrases verbatim, because the comprehended content cannot be relayed to the motor speech area for direct repetition. This selective repetition deficit, out of proportion to otherwise near-normal language function, is the hallmark that distinguishes conduction aphasia from both Broca's and Wernicke's aphasia.
concepts.explicit_objective: Identify impaired repetition, with preserved fluency and comprehension, as the hallmark of conduction aphasia.
concepts.module_subject: ASU-CNS-3 > Physiology > Language and higher cortical function
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing conduction aphasia (fluent speech and comprehension, isolated repetition deficit, arcuate fasciculus lesion) with Broca's aphasia (non-fluent speech, comprehension relatively preserved) or Wernicke's aphasia (fluent but meaningless speech, poor comprehension).
concepts.original_wording: Source item 27 ("Cannot Repeat words: Conductive aphasia"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf, p3.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 27 of EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf (src_85504e7525d793760af2), p3.

concepts.label: The excitatory (ascending activating) reticular formation shows spontaneous, intrinsic neuronal activity independent of external sensory input
concepts.article_title: Intrinsic activity of the excitatory reticular formation
concepts.definition: The excitatory component of the reticular formation, which forms the core of the ascending reticular activating system (ARAS) maintaining cortical arousal and wakefulness, is characterised by intrinsic, spontaneous (pacemaker-like) neuronal firing that does not require continuous sensory input to sustain it, unlike purely sensory relay neurons whose activity depends on afferent drive. This intrinsic excitability allows the ARAS to maintain a baseline level of cortical arousal even in the relative absence of external stimulation, and explains why it can be modulated (facilitated or depressed) by anaesthetic agents and sedatives acting directly on these neurons rather than only on their sensory inputs.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that the excitatory reticular formation has intrinsic, spontaneous activity independent of sensory input.
concepts.module_subject: ASU-CNS-3 > Physiology > Reticular formation and consciousness
concepts.pitfalls: Assuming the reticular formation's excitatory activity is entirely driven by ongoing sensory input, rather than recognising its intrinsic, self-sustaining pacemaker-like firing.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 28 ("Reticular excitatory : has intrinsic activity"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf, p3.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 28 of EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf (src_85504e7525d793760af2), p3.

concepts.label: The lamina terminalis forms the anterior wall of the third ventricle
concepts.article_title: Lamina terminalis: anterior third ventricle wall
concepts.definition: The lamina terminalis is a thin sheet of grey matter extending from the anterior commissure above to the optic chiasm below, and it forms the anterior wall of the third ventricle, closing off the rostral end of the embryonic neural tube at this level. It is functionally important as one of the circumventricular organs' neighbouring structures and as a site where the vascular organ of the lamina terminalis (OVLT), lacking a normal blood-brain barrier, contributes to fluid balance and thermoregulatory sensing. Surgically, the lamina terminalis can be opened (lamina terminalis fenestration) as a route for CSF diversion in some third-ventricular procedures.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that the lamina terminalis forms the anterior wall of the third ventricle.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing the lamina terminalis (anterior wall of the third ventricle) with the anterior commissure or optic chiasm, the two structures that bound it above and below.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 30 ("Anterior of 3rd ventricle:Lamina Terminalis"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf, p3.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 30 of EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf (src_85504e7525d793760af2), p3.

concepts.label: Aminoglycosides are given intrathecally to treat CNS infection because they penetrate the blood-brain barrier poorly by the intravenous route
concepts.definition: Aminoglycosides are highly polar, water-soluble antibiotics that cross the intact (or even inflamed) blood-brain barrier poorly when given intravenously, so achieving therapeutic CSF concentrations by the systemic route alone is unreliable, particularly for resistant Gram-negative CNS infections such as multidrug-resistant Gram-negative ventriculitis or meningitis. In these situations, aminoglycosides are administered directly into the CSF space by the intrathecal or intraventricular route, bypassing the blood-brain barrier entirely and achieving high local concentrations while limiting systemic nephro- and ototoxicity. This is a distinct route decision from most other CNS-active antibiotics (e.g. third-generation cephalosporins), which achieve adequate CSF levels via the IV route alone when meninges are inflamed.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that aminoglycosides are given intrathecally for CNS infection because of poor blood-brain barrier penetration by the IV route.
concepts.pitfalls: Assuming all antibiotics need the intrathecal route for CNS infection, rather than recognising that aminoglycosides specifically need it because of their poor blood-brain barrier penetration by the IV route, unlike agents such as third-generation cephalosporins.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 32 ("Antibiotic taken intrathecal: Aminoglycoside"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf, p3.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 32 of EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf (src_85504e7525d793760af2), p3.

concepts.label: The EEG records the summated spontaneous postsynaptic potentials of cortical pyramidal neurons, not action potentials
concepts.definition: The electroencephalogram (EEG) records the ongoing (spontaneous) electrical activity of the cerebral cortex, and its scalp-recorded waveforms reflect the summation of postsynaptic (excitatory and inhibitory) potentials generated synchronously in the apical dendrites of large populations of cortical pyramidal neurons, aligned in parallel radial columns. Individual axonal action potentials are too brief, too asynchronous, and too poorly aligned in orientation to summate into a detectable scalp signal, so the EEG specifically reflects this spontaneous graded synaptic activity rather than spike (action potential) activity. This is why EEG frequency and amplitude change with the level of synchronisation and arousal, rather than with individual neuronal firing rates alone.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that the EEG reflects summated, spontaneous postsynaptic potentials of cortical pyramidal neurons rather than action potentials.
concepts.module_subject: ASU-CNS-3 > Physiology > EEG and cortical electrophysiology
concepts.pitfalls: Assuming the EEG records action potentials directly, rather than the summated, spontaneous postsynaptic potentials of synchronised cortical pyramidal neurons.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 33 ("EEG: spontaneous potential"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf, p3.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 33 of EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf (src_85504e7525d793760af2), p3.

concepts.label: Zolpidem is a non-benzodiazepine GABA-A receptor agonist used as a hypnotic
concepts.article_title: Zolpidem as a GABA-A agonist hypnotic
concepts.definition: Zolpidem is an imidazopyridine, non-benzodiazepine hypnotic that acts as a positive allosteric modulator (agonist) at the benzodiazepine site of the GABA-A receptor, with relative selectivity for the alpha-1 subunit-containing receptor subtype that mediates sedative-hypnotic effects. This selectivity gives zolpidem strong sedative-hypnotic potency for short-term insomnia treatment with comparatively less anxiolytic, myorelaxant and anticonvulsant activity than classic benzodiazepines, which act more broadly across alpha subunit subtypes. It shares the underlying GABA-A receptor mechanism with benzodiazepines but is structurally and pharmacologically distinct from them.
concepts.explicit_objective: Identify zolpidem as a non-benzodiazepine GABA-A receptor agonist used for its hypnotic effect.
concepts.pitfalls: Classifying zolpidem as a benzodiazepine rather than a distinct, alpha-1-selective non-benzodiazepine GABA-A agonist; its alpha-1 selectivity also makes its anticonvulsant activity weaker and less clinically relied-upon than that of classic benzodiazepines.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 34 ("GABA agonist+Anticonvulsant:Zolpidem"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf, p3.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 34 of EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf (src_85504e7525d793760af2), p3. Printed key pairs zolpidem with "anticonvulsant"; standard teaching emphasises zolpidem's alpha-1-selective hypnotic action, with anticonvulsant use far less established than for classic benzodiazepines — this concept authors the well-supported GABA-A-agonist-hypnotic claim and flags the anticonvulsant pairing as a doubtful extension rather than asserting it as fact.

concepts.label: Ketamine is the preferred induction anaesthetic for hypotensive or haemodynamically unstable patients because it raises or maintains blood pressure
concepts.definition: Ketamine, an NMDA receptor antagonist, is distinctive among induction anaesthetics because it stimulates the sympathetic nervous system (by inhibiting neuronal catecholamine reuptake), producing a rise in heart rate, blood pressure and cardiac output, in contrast to agents such as propofol or thiopental that cause dose-dependent myocardial depression and vasodilation. This sympathomimetic profile makes ketamine the preferred induction agent in hypotensive, hypovolaemic or haemodynamically unstable patients (e.g. trauma, shock), where further blood-pressure depression from other agents would be dangerous. Its dissociative anaesthetic and analgesic properties, alongside preserved airway reflexes, further support its use in emergency and field settings.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that ketamine is favoured for anaesthesia in hypotensive patients because of its sympathomimetic, blood-pressure-supporting effect.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing ketamine's sympathomimetic, blood-pressure-supporting profile with the myocardial-depressant, hypotension-inducing effect of most other IV induction agents such as propofol or thiopental.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 35 ("Anesthesia for HypOtension:Ketamine"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf, p3.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 35 of EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf (src_85504e7525d793760af2), p3.

concepts.label: Lidocaine, a class Ib antiarrhythmic, is used to treat ventricular arrhythmias occurring under anaesthesia
concepts.definition: Lidocaine is a class Ib antiarrhythmic that blocks fast voltage-gated sodium channels preferentially in ischaemic or depolarised (fast-firing) myocardial tissue, shortening the action potential and suppressing ventricular ectopic activity, and it is used intravenously to treat ventricular arrhythmias (e.g. ventricular tachycardia or ectopy) that arise during anaesthesia, such as those triggered by laryngoscopy, intubation or catecholamine surges. Because it has minimal effect on atrial tissue and normal conduction, it is selectively useful for ventricular arrhythmias rather than as a broad-spectrum antiarrhythmic. Its local anaesthetic and antiarrhythmic actions share the same underlying sodium-channel-blocking mechanism.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that lidocaine's class Ib antiarrhythmic action is used to treat ventricular arrhythmias occurring during anaesthesia.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing lidocaine's selective usefulness for ventricular (not atrial) arrhythmias with a broad-spectrum antiarrhythmic action, and separating its antiarrhythmic use from its more familiar local anaesthetic use, which share the same sodium-channel mechanism.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 36 ("Cardiac arrhythmia anesthesia:Lidocaine"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf, p3.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 36 of EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf (src_85504e7525d793760af2), p3.

concepts.label: Carbamazepine causes dilutional hyponatraemia by inducing a syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH)
concepts.definition: Carbamazepine, an antiepileptic that blocks voltage-gated sodium channels, characteristically produces a syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH)-like effect, potentiating the action of (or directly stimulating release of) antidiuretic hormone at the renal collecting duct, causing excessive free-water retention and consequent dilutional hyponatraemia. This is a well-recognised, dose-related adverse effect requiring periodic serum sodium monitoring during carbamazepine therapy, particularly in elderly patients or those on other drugs that also lower sodium. It contrasts with other antiepileptics' more mechanistically distinct adverse-effect profiles (e.g. valproate's teratogenicity or phenytoin's gingival hyperplasia).
concepts.explicit_objective: State that carbamazepine causes dilutional hyponatraemia through an SIADH-like mechanism.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing carbamazepine's SIADH-like hyponatraemia with other antiepileptics' distinct characteristic adverse effects (e.g. valproate's teratogenicity, phenytoin's gingival hyperplasia).
concepts.original_wording: Source item 37 ("Dilutional hyponateremia :Carbamazepine"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf, p3.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 37 of EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf (src_85504e7525d793760af2), p3.

concepts.label: The categorical (dominant) hemisphere specialises in language and mathematical/analytic operations
concepts.definition: The two cerebral hemispheres are functionally lateralised: the categorical (dominant, usually left) hemisphere specialises in sequential, analytic processing, including language, calculation and logical/mathematical operations, while the representational (non-dominant, usually right) hemisphere specialises in holistic, spatial and non-verbal processing such as facial recognition, spatial construction and musical/artistic perception. This categorical-hemisphere role in mathematical operations parallels its role in language, both reflecting a shared underlying capacity for sequential, rule-based symbolic processing. Damage to the categorical hemisphere's parietal association cortex (e.g. angular gyrus) can therefore impair calculation (acalculia) alongside language deficits, as part of Gerstmann syndrome.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that the categorical (dominant) hemisphere specialises in mathematical/analytic operations, alongside language.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing the categorical (dominant) hemisphere's analytic/mathematical/language specialisation with the representational (non-dominant) hemisphere's holistic/spatial/facial-recognition specialisation.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 41 ("Categorical hemisphere:Mathematical operations"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf, p4.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 41 of EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf (src_85504e7525d793760af2), p4.

concepts.label: Flaccid dysarthria, from a lower motor neuron lesion, produces weak, breathy, hypernasal speech
concepts.definition: Flaccid dysarthria results from a lower motor neuron lesion affecting the cranial nerves or nuclei that supply the muscles of speech articulation and phonation (e.g. bulbar palsy affecting the vagus, glossopharyngeal or hypoglossal nuclei), producing weak, breathy and hypernasal ("nasal-sounding") speech because of weakness of the soft palate and pharyngeal muscles that fail to seal off the nasal cavity during speech. This LMN, hypernasal, weak pattern contrasts with the strained, harsh quality of spastic dysarthria from an upper motor neuron (pseudobulbar) lesion, in which the muscles are weak but hypertonic rather than flaccid. Distinguishing the two patterns helps localise bulbar dysfunction to an LMN versus UMN lesion.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that flaccid (LMN) dysarthria produces weak, hypernasal speech, distinct from spastic (UMN) dysarthria.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing flaccid (LMN, weak and hypernasal) dysarthria with spastic (UMN/pseudobulbar, strained-harsh) dysarthria.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 42 ("Flaccid dysarthria:weak nasal speech"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf, p4.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 42 of EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf (src_85504e7525d793760af2), p4.

concepts.label: Temperature regulation is not a core limbic system function; it is chiefly a hypothalamic homeostatic function
concepts.article_title: Temperature regulation is not a limbic function
concepts.definition: The limbic system (hippocampus, amygdala, cingulate gyrus, septal area, and connected structures) is classically defined by its roles in emotion, motivation, memory formation and behavioural drive states, not by autonomic homeostatic regulation such as body temperature control, which is instead the specific responsibility of the hypothalamus's preoptic/anterior region (heat loss) and posterior region (heat conservation). While the hypothalamus is anatomically and functionally linked to the limbic system as part of the extended limbic circuitry, temperature regulation itself is attributed specifically to the hypothalamic thermoregulatory centres rather than being classed as a limbic (emotional/memory) function. This distinction is a common examiner's "which function does NOT belong" question testing whether students over-generalise all hypothalamic-linked functions as limbic.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that temperature regulation is a hypothalamic homeostatic function, not a core limbic system (emotion/memory) function.
concepts.module_subject: ASU-CNS-3 > Anatomy > Limbic system and emotion
concepts.pitfalls: Over-generalising every hypothalamus-linked function as "limbic", rather than distinguishing the limbic system's core emotion/memory/motivation roles from the hypothalamus's separate homeostatic roles such as thermoregulation.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 43 ("Function not related to Limbic:Temperature regulation"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf, p4.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 43 of EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf (src_85504e7525d793760af2), p4.

concepts.label: Stimulation of the periventricular (medial hypothalamic) region produces aversive, punishment-like responses
concepts.article_title: Periventricular hypothalamus and the punishment centre
concepts.definition: Classic self-stimulation studies (building on the reward-centre work of Olds and Milner) identified that electrical stimulation of the periventricular zone and medial hypothalamic region produces avoidance, fear and aversive ("punishment-centre") behavioural responses, in contrast to stimulation of the lateral hypothalamus and medial forebrain bundle, which produces pleasurable, reward-seeking behaviour that animals will repeatedly self-stimulate to obtain. This punishment/reward dichotomy within the hypothalamus is a standard physiology teaching point on the neural substrates of motivated behaviour. The periventricular punishment system is thought to interact with the amygdala's fear-related circuitry, part of the broader limbic apparatus governing aversive emotional responses.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that the periventricular (medial) hypothalamic region mediates aversive, punishment-type responses, contrasted with the lateral hypothalamic reward system.
concepts.module_subject: ASU-CNS-3 > Anatomy > Limbic system and emotion
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing the periventricular/medial hypothalamic "punishment" region with the lateral hypothalamic/medial forebrain bundle "reward" (pleasure) region, which produce opposite behavioural responses on stimulation.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 44 ("Periventricular nucleus :Aversion (Punishment)"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf, p4.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 44 of EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf (src_85504e7525d793760af2), p4.

concepts.label: Semantic memory is the long-term memory system for general facts and knowledge, distinct from episodic memory of personal events
concepts.definition: Declarative (explicit) long-term memory is divided into semantic memory, the store of general facts, concepts and "basic knowledge" about the world (e.g. that Cairo is the capital of Egypt) held without reference to when or where it was learned, and episodic memory, the store of personally experienced events tied to a specific time and place. Semantic memory is relatively resistant to the effects of normal ageing and even to some forms of amnesia that preferentially disrupt episodic recall, reflecting at least partly separable neural substrates. This distinction underlies why patients with certain hippocampal-predominant amnesias can still access well-established general knowledge while losing the ability to recall recent personal experiences.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that semantic memory is the declarative memory system for general factual ("basic") knowledge, distinct from episodic memory.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing semantic memory (general factual knowledge, not tied to a specific personal event) with episodic memory (personally experienced events tied to time and place).
concepts.original_wording: Source item 45 ("Basic knowledge:Semantic memory"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf, p4.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 45 of EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf (src_85504e7525d793760af2), p4.

concepts.label: Retrograde amnesia is the loss of memories formed before the injury, distinct from anterograde amnesia's loss of new memory formation after it
concepts.article_title: Retrograde amnesia: memories lost before injury
concepts.definition: Retrograde amnesia is the inability to recall memories or events that were formed before a brain injury or insult (e.g. head trauma, hypoxic episode), reflecting disruption of previously consolidated (or still-consolidating) memory traces, and it classically shows a temporal gradient in which more remote memories are better preserved than memories from just before the injury. This contrasts with anterograde amnesia, the inability to form new memories after the injury, which reflects failure of ongoing memory consolidation rather than loss of previously stored memories. Many amnestic syndromes (e.g. after significant head trauma) produce a mixed picture with both retrograde and anterograde components.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that retrograde amnesia is the loss of memories formed before an injury, distinct from anterograde amnesia.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing retrograde amnesia (loss of pre-injury memories) with anterograde amnesia (failure to form new memories after the injury).
concepts.original_wording: Source item 46 ("Injury then lost memory: Retrograde amnesia"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf, p4.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 46 of EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf (src_85504e7525d793760af2), p4.

concepts.label: Mirtazapine is an antidepressant with a distinct (NaSSA) mechanism, used as an alternative to SSRIs such as sertraline
concepts.definition: Mirtazapine is a noradrenergic and specific serotonergic antidepressant (NaSSA) that works by antagonising presynaptic alpha-2 adrenergic autoreceptors (increasing noradrenaline and serotonin release) and blocking specific postsynaptic serotonin receptors (5-HT2 and 5-HT3), a mechanism entirely distinct from the serotonin-reuptake-inhibition mechanism of SSRIs such as sertraline. Its sedating and appetite-stimulating side-effect profile (via histamine H1 antagonism) makes it a useful alternative or adjunct in depressed patients with insomnia or weight loss, where an SSRI's typical activating, appetite-suppressing profile would be less desirable. It is grouped among the non-SSRI antidepressants used when SSRI therapy is ineffective or poorly tolerated.
concepts.explicit_objective: Identify mirtazapine as a non-SSRI (NaSSA) antidepressant used as an alternative to SSRIs such as sertraline.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing mirtazapine's NaSSA mechanism (alpha-2 autoreceptor antagonism plus 5-HT2/5-HT3 blockade) with the serotonin-reuptake-inhibition mechanism of SSRIs such as sertraline.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 48 ("Antidepressants other than sertaline (SSRI): Mertazapine"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf, p4.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 48 of EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf (src_85504e7525d793760af2), p4.

concepts.label: Bupropion, an antidepressant, is also approved for smoking cessation
concepts.definition: Bupropion is a norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor (NDRI) antidepressant that, separately from its antidepressant use, is also approved (marketed as Zyban for this indication) for smoking cessation, where it reduces nicotine craving and withdrawal symptoms, likely through its dopaminergic and noradrenergic activity mimicking some of nicotine's reward-pathway effects. It carries a lower risk of sexual dysfunction and weight gain than SSRIs, and it lowers the seizure threshold, so it is used cautiously in patients with a seizure history. Its dual antidepressant/smoking-cessation use is a distinctive feature among antidepressants, most of which lack this addiction-medicine indication.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that bupropion is used for smoking cessation, in addition to its antidepressant indication.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing bupropion (NDRI antidepressant, also used for smoking cessation) with varenicline, the other classic smoking-cessation drug, which instead works as a partial nicotinic receptor agonist.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 49 ("Antidepressants +Smoking Cessation:Bupropion"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf, p4.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 49 of EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf (src_85504e7525d793760af2), p4.

concepts.label: The sensory (dorsal horn) part of the developing spinal cord arises from the alar lamina of the neural tube
concepts.article_title: Alar lamina and the sensory spinal cord
concepts.definition: The developing neural tube's spinal cord region is divided by the sulcus limitans into a dorsal alar lamina and a ventral basal lamina; the alar lamina gives rise to the sensory (afferent) dorsal horn neurons of the mature spinal cord, while the basal lamina gives rise to the motor (efferent) ventral horn neurons. This dorsal-sensory/ventral-motor organisation, established embryologically by the alar/basal lamina division, is the developmental basis for the adult spinal cord's dorsal (sensory) versus ventral (motor) horn arrangement. The same alar/basal division extends into the brainstem, where it underlies the sensory-dorsal/motor-ventral organisation of the cranial nerve nuclear columns.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that the sensory (dorsal horn) part of the spinal cord derives embryologically from the alar lamina of the neural tube.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing the alar lamina (dorsal, gives rise to sensory dorsal horn) with the basal lamina (ventral, gives rise to motor ventral horn) of the developing neural tube.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 50 ("Sensory part of spinal cord is made from Alar lamina (embryology)"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf, p4.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 50 of EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf (src_85504e7525d793760af2), p4.

concepts.label: Cerebrospinal fluid is absorbed into the venous blood of the dural sinuses through the arachnoid villi
concepts.definition: Cerebrospinal fluid, produced chiefly by the choroid plexus, is reabsorbed back into the systemic venous circulation through arachnoid villi (and their larger clusters, the arachnoid granulations), finger-like projections of the arachnoid mater that protrude into the venous sinuses, principally the superior sagittal sinus. These villi act as one-way pressure-sensitive valves, allowing bulk flow of CSF into venous blood when CSF pressure exceeds venous sinus pressure, but preventing back-flow of blood into the subarachnoid space. Obstruction or reduced function of the arachnoid villi (e.g. after meningitis or subarachnoid haemorrhage) is a classic mechanism of communicating hydrocephalus.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that CSF drains into the venous sinuses (chiefly the superior sagittal sinus) through the arachnoid villi.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing arachnoid villi (the site of CSF absorption into venous blood) with the choroid plexus (the site of CSF production), the two ends of CSF circulation.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 51 ("CSF is drained in blood through:Arachnoid villi"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf, p4.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 51 of EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf (src_85504e7525d793760af2), p4.

concepts.label: Tetanus toxin (tetanospasmin) blocks the release of inhibitory neurotransmitters (glycine and GABA) at spinal inhibitory synapses
concepts.article_title: Tetanus toxin and inhibitory synapse blockade
concepts.definition: Tetanospasmin, the neurotoxin of Clostridium tetani, travels retrogradely along motor axons and transsynaptically into inhibitory interneurons (including Renshaw cells) in the spinal cord and brainstem, where it cleaves synaptobrevin (VAMP), a protein required for synaptic vesicle docking and fusion, blocking the release of the inhibitory neurotransmitters glycine and GABA. Loss of this normal inhibitory restraint on motor neurons produces uncontrolled, simultaneous contraction of agonist and antagonist muscles, manifesting clinically as the sustained muscle spasms (trismus/lockjaw, opisthotonus, generalised rigidity) characteristic of tetanus. This mechanism mirrors botulinum toxin's cleavage of similar vesicle-fusion proteins, but botulinum acts at the neuromuscular junction on excitatory (acetylcholine-releasing) synapses rather than on inhibitory CNS synapses, producing flaccid rather than spastic paralysis.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that tetanus toxin blocks release of the inhibitory neurotransmitters glycine and GABA at spinal inhibitory synapses.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing tetanus toxin's CNS action (blocking inhibitory glycine/GABA release, causing spastic paralysis) with botulinum toxin's peripheral neuromuscular-junction action (blocking excitatory acetylcholine release, causing flaccid paralysis).
concepts.original_wording: Source item 52 ("Clostridia Tetanai mechanism: Block inhibitory synapse"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf, p4-5.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 52 of EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf (src_85504e7525d793760af2), p4-5. This concept covers the toxin's mechanism of action (a physiology/pharmacology teaching point), not organism classification, which is out of this lane's neuro subject scope.

concepts.label: An unvaccinated person exposed to rabies requires both rabies immunoglobulin and rabies vaccine
concepts.article_title: Post-exposure rabies prophylaxis in the unvaccinated
concepts.definition: In a previously unvaccinated person exposed to a potentially rabid animal, post-exposure prophylaxis requires both passive immunisation with rabies immunoglobulin (infiltrated around the wound and given intramuscularly, providing immediate neutralising antibody before the person's own immune response can develop) and active immunisation with a full course of rabies vaccine (stimulating the person's own long-lasting antibody response). Rabies immunoglobulin is specifically omitted in previously vaccinated individuals, who only require booster vaccine doses, since they already have primed immunity. Because rabies encephalitis is essentially universally fatal once symptoms begin, this combined immediate prophylaxis is critical and time-sensitive.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that an unvaccinated person exposed to rabies needs both rabies immunoglobulin and rabies vaccine.
concepts.pitfalls: Forgetting that rabies immunoglobulin is only needed in previously unvaccinated patients; a previously vaccinated person requires booster vaccine doses alone, without immunoglobulin.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 53 ("Rabies+UnVaccinated= Rabies immunoglobulins &vaccine"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf, p5.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 53 of EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf (src_85504e7525d793760af2), p5. This concept covers the post-exposure treatment protocol (a pharmacology/clinical-management teaching point), distinct from the excluded general-microbiology/community-medicine items in this same source.

concepts.label: Acute attacks of multiple sclerosis are treated with high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone
concepts.article_title: IV methylprednisolone for acute MS relapse
concepts.definition: An acute relapse (attack) of multiple sclerosis is treated with a short course of high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone, a potent glucocorticoid that reduces the acute CNS inflammation and oedema underlying the new or worsening neurological deficit, thereby shortening the duration and severity of the relapse. This acute anti-inflammatory treatment is distinct from the disease-modifying therapies (e.g. interferon-beta, natalizumab) used for long-term relapse prevention, and IV methylprednisolone does not itself alter the long-term disease course. Because corticosteroids do not reverse the underlying demyelinating pathology, their role is specifically to hasten recovery from the acute inflammatory episode.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that acute attacks of multiple sclerosis are treated with high-dose IV methylprednisolone.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing IV methylprednisolone's role in treating the acute inflammatory relapse with the separate, long-term disease-modifying therapies used to reduce future relapse frequency.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 54 ("Acute Attacks of Multiple sclerosis:Methylpredinisone(IV)"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf, p5.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 54 of EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf (src_85504e7525d793760af2), p5.

concepts.label: Fluconazole is used for maintenance (suppressive) therapy of CNS cryptococcal infection after initial induction treatment
concepts.article_title: Fluconazole maintenance therapy for cryptococcal meningitis
concepts.definition: Treatment of cryptococcal meningitis (a classic opportunistic CNS fungal infection in immunocompromised, particularly AIDS, patients) follows an induction-consolidation-maintenance strategy: induction with amphotericin B plus flucytosine to rapidly reduce fungal burden, followed by consolidation and then long-term maintenance (suppressive) therapy with oral fluconazole, which is well tolerated and CNS-penetrant enough for prolonged use but less potent than amphotericin B for the acute infection. This maintenance phase is continued until the patient's immune status has sufficiently recovered (e.g. sustained CD4 count rise on antiretroviral therapy), to prevent relapse. Fluconazole's oral bioavailability and good CSF penetration make it well suited to this long-term suppressive role.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that fluconazole is used for maintenance/suppressive therapy of CNS cryptococcal infection after amphotericin-based induction treatment.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing fluconazole's maintenance/suppressive role (after induction) with amphotericin B's role as the potent induction agent for acute cryptococcal meningitis.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 56 ("Maintained drug for Fungal infection:Fluconazole"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf, p5.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 56 of EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf (src_85504e7525d793760af2), p5. Printed key does not name the specific fungal infection; this concept frames it as CNS cryptococcal meningitis maintenance therapy, the standard exam context for this fact, and flags the assumption here rather than silently guessing.

concepts.label: Subdural haemorrhage results from tearing of the bridging (cortical) veins that cross the subdural space
concepts.article_title: Subdural haemorrhage from bridging vein tears
concepts.definition: Bridging (cortical) veins drain the surface of the cerebral cortex and cross the subdural space to empty into the dural venous sinuses (chiefly the superior sagittal sinus); because they traverse this space largely unsupported, they are vulnerable to tearing from shearing forces during head trauma, particularly with rapid deceleration, and their rupture is the classic mechanism of subdural haemorrhage. This contrasts with epidural (extradural) haemorrhage, most often caused by tearing of the middle meningeal artery after a temporal bone fracture, giving the two haemorrhage types distinct vessels, spaces and clinical time-courses (subdural bleeding often slower and more insidious, given its lower-pressure venous source). Elderly and alcoholic patients, with cerebral atrophy that stretches the bridging veins, are especially predisposed to subdural haemorrhage even after relatively minor trauma.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that subdural haemorrhage results from tearing of the bridging veins crossing the subdural space.
concepts.subtopic: Venous drainage of the head and neck
concepts.module_subject: ASU-CNS-3 > Anatomy > Venous drainage of the head and neck
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing subdural haemorrhage's venous (bridging vein) mechanism with epidural haemorrhage's arterial (middle meningeal artery) mechanism, the two classically contrasted traumatic intracranial bleeds.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 61 ("Subdural hge: Tear of bridging veins"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf, p5.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 61 of EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf (src_85504e7525d793760af2), p5.

concepts.label: Von Hippel-Lindau disease, an autosomal dominant syndrome, links renal cell carcinoma with CNS haemangioblastomas, so a family history matters
concepts.article_title: Von Hippel-Lindau disease and renal cell carcinoma
concepts.definition: Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease is an autosomal dominant tumour-suppressor syndrome (VHL gene, chromosome 3p) that predisposes patients to clear-cell renal cell carcinoma together with CNS and retinal haemangioblastomas (classically of the cerebellum), phaeochromocytoma and other cystic/tumour lesions. Because of its autosomal dominant inheritance, a patient presenting with renal cell carcinoma and a positive family history should prompt consideration of underlying VHL disease and screening for its other manifestations, including CNS haemangioblastoma, rather than treating the renal tumour as an isolated sporadic finding. This link between a CNS-related genetic tumour syndrome and renal cell carcinoma is a classic multi-system association tested in oncology/pathology teaching.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that von Hippel-Lindau disease, an autosomal dominant syndrome causing CNS haemangioblastomas, is associated with renal cell carcinoma, especially with a positive family history.
concepts.pitfalls: Treating renal cell carcinoma with a positive family history as an isolated sporadic finding rather than considering the autosomal dominant VHL syndrome, which also predisposes to CNS haemangioblastoma.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 62 ("Renal cell carcinoma +Family history:VHL von hippel ds"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf, p5.

Printed item does not itself name a CNS lesion; this concept frames the fact through VHL's defining CNS haemangioblastoma association, the standard reason this item appears in a CNS paper, and flags that framing here rather than silently assuming it.

concepts.label: Clozapine, an atypical antipsychotic, carries a risk of life-threatening agranulocytosis requiring regular blood count monitoring
concepts.definition: Clozapine, an atypical antipsychotic reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia because of its superior efficacy, carries a well-known risk of agranulocytosis (severe neutropenia), a potentially life-threatening adverse effect that mandates regular absolute neutrophil count monitoring throughout treatment, with mandatory dose interruption or discontinuation if counts fall below defined thresholds. This risk is a defining feature that distinguishes clozapine's safety profile from other atypical antipsychotics, and is the reason clozapine is not used as a first-line agent despite its strong efficacy in resistant cases. The exact mechanism is thought to involve toxic or immune-mediated injury to bone marrow granulocyte precursors.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that clozapine carries a risk of agranulocytosis, requiring regular neutrophil count monitoring.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing clozapine's defining agranulocytosis risk (requiring blood count monitoring) with the extrapyramidal side effects more characteristic of typical antipsychotics, which clozapine itself largely avoids.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 65 ("Agranulocytosis:Clonazpine (antipsychotic)"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf, p5.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 65 of EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf (src_85504e7525d793760af2), p5. Printed key spells the drug "Clonazpine"; agranulocytosis is the classic adverse effect of clozapine (an antipsychotic), not clonazepam (a benzodiazepine) — the source's own "(antipsychotic)" annotation confirms clozapine was intended, so this concept is authored under the corrected spelling.

concepts.label: The hypoglossal nerve supplies motor innervation to the muscles of the tongue
concepts.definition: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) provides motor innervation to nearly all the intrinsic and extrinsic muscles of the tongue (genioglossus, hyoglossus, styloglossus and the intrinsic tongue muscles), the single exception being palatoglossus, which is instead supplied by the vagus nerve (via the pharyngeal plexus, carrying fibres from the cranial accessory) because it develops from pharyngeal arch mesenchyme rather than occipital myotomes. A unilateral hypoglossal nerve lesion produces ipsilateral tongue weakness and wasting, with the protruded tongue deviating toward the side of the lesion because of the unopposed action of the healthy-side genioglossus. This near-total but not absolute rule (excepting palatoglossus) is a classic anatomy exam nuance.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that the hypoglossal nerve supplies motor innervation to the muscles of the tongue, with palatoglossus as the exception.
concepts.module_subject: ASU-CNS-3 > Anatomy > Cranial nerve motor supply
concepts.pitfalls: Forgetting that palatoglossus is the one tongue muscle NOT supplied by the hypoglossal nerve, being supplied instead by the vagus nerve via the pharyngeal plexus.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 67 ("Hypoglossal nerves supply tongue ms"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf, p6.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 67 of EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf (src_85504e7525d793760af2), p6.

concepts.label: The chorda tympani carries preganglionic parasympathetic fibres to the submandibular ganglion, supplying the submandibular and sublingual glands
concepts.definition: The chorda tympani, a branch of the facial nerve (CN VII) carrying preganglionic parasympathetic fibres from the superior salivatory nucleus, joins the lingual nerve (a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve) and travels with it to reach the submandibular ganglion, where it synapses; postganglionic fibres from this ganglion then supply secretomotor innervation to the submandibular and sublingual salivary glands. The chorda tympani also carries special sensory (taste) fibres from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, making it a mixed nerve with both a distinct secretomotor and a distinct gustatory function along the same short course through the middle ear. Its close relationship to the lingual nerve, despite arising from a different cranial nerve, is a classic anatomical pairing tested in this region.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that the chorda tympani carries preganglionic parasympathetic fibres to the submandibular ganglion, supplying the submandibular and sublingual glands.
concepts.module_subject: ASU-CNS-3 > Anatomy > Parasympathetic pathways of the head
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing the chorda tympani's route (joining the lingual nerve to reach the submandibular ganglion, supplying submandibular/sublingual glands) with the greater petrosal nerve's separate route to the pterygopalatine ganglion, which instead supplies the lacrimal and nasal glands.

concepts.label: Microglia are the resident macrophages of the central nervous system
concepts.definition: Microglia are the resident immune cells of the CNS, functioning as tissue-resident macrophages: unlike astrocytes, oligodendrocytes and ependymal cells, which arise from neuroectoderm, microglia derive from mesodermal yolk-sac myeloid progenitors that colonise the CNS during early development, giving them a monocyte/macrophage lineage distinct from the other neuroglia. In their resting (ramified) state they continually survey the CNS parenchyma, and upon injury, infection or degeneration they become activated, transforming into an amoeboid, phagocytic form that clears cellular debris, pathogens and misfolded proteins, and that also presents antigen and releases inflammatory mediators. This macrophage-equivalent phagocytic and immune-surveillance role is the defining functional feature that separates microglia from the other, structural/supportive glial cell types.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that microglia are the CNS-resident macrophages, functionally and developmentally distinct from the neuroectoderm-derived glia.
concepts.module_subject: ASU-CNS-3 > Histology > Neuroglia and blood-brain barrier
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing microglia's mesodermal, monocyte/macrophage-lineage origin and phagocytic immune role with the neuroectoderm-derived, structural/supportive roles of astrocytes, oligodendrocytes and ependymal cells.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 72 ("Microglia functionally as macrophages"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf, p6.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 72 of EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf (src_85504e7525d793760af2), p6.

concepts.label: The anterior nucleus of the thalamus is connected to the mammillary bodies via the mammillothalamic tract, as part of the Papez circuit
concepts.article_title: Anterior thalamic nucleus and the mammillary bodies
concepts.definition: The anterior nucleus of the thalamus receives a major direct input from the mammillary bodies of the hypothalamus via the mammillothalamic tract (the tract of Vicq d'Azyr), a specific white-matter connection that forms one link of the Papez circuit (hippocampus to fornix to mammillary bodies to mammillothalamic tract to anterior thalamic nucleus to cingulate gyrus). The anterior nucleus then projects onward to the cingulate gyrus via the anterior thalamic radiation, continuing the circuit's role in memory consolidation and emotional processing. This mammillothalamic connection is clinically relevant because lesions here (e.g. in Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, which damages the mammillary bodies) disrupt this specific relay and contribute to the resulting anterograde amnesia.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that the anterior thalamic nucleus receives input from the mammillary bodies via the mammillothalamic tract, as part of the Papez circuit.
concepts.module_subject: ASU-CNS-3 > Anatomy > Limbic system and emotion
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing the mammillothalamic tract's specific mammillary-body-to-anterior-thalamic-nucleus connection with the fornix, the Papez circuit's separate hippocampus-to-mammillary-body link.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 73 ("Anterior nucleus of thalamus connected with Mammillary Bodies"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf, p6.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 73 of EOM - CNS paper 2 2018.pdf (src_85504e7525d793760af2), p6. Covers a specific anatomical connection within the Papez circuit, distinct from this lane's existing concept on the circuit's overall emotional function.
